## What may be a BLOCKER

A blocker REJECTS the implementer's work and forces another attempt. It must therefore be something that implementer can actually do. Before raising one, check all three:

1. IS IT IN THE PLAN? The root-cause analysis above is the plan of record — the same one the implementer was given. A blocker must concern a file that plan names. If you believe work is needed somewhere the plan does not mention, that is a finding about the PLAN, not a failure by the implementer: raise it as an ADVISORY note beginning 'SPEC:' and explain what the plan appears to be missing. Do NOT describe it as 'prescribed' or 'required' — the implementer will follow you out of scope, and the change will be rejected later for exceeding the plan. For this project, plans are domain-isolated: MOCK3-1 (fares) lives entirely within mocka, and MOCK3-2 (schedule) lives entirely within mockb. Do not require changes across codelines.

2. DOES THE PLAN EXEMPT IT? A site marked NO EDIT REQUIRED is part of the fix and correctly left untouched. Never raise a finding of any severity because such a file is unchanged. The implementer was told not to change it.

3. CAN IT BE SATISFIED? If you claim something is missing — a package, a file, an export, an API — CONFIRM IT with the tools you have before raising it. A blocker naming a dependency that does not exist, or an API the installed version does not provide, can never be resolved: the implementer will fail on it repeatedly and the story will exhaust its attempts on your mistake. For this project, verify that fixes can run under vitest and that TypeScript type-checks cleanly in the affected codeline.

4. IS IT INSIDE THE PLAN? A file the plan NAMES, and does not mark NO EDIT REQUIRED, was PRESCRIBED. Changing it is compliance, not over-engineering. Never raise a finding of any severity because a prescribed file was changed, and never assert a smaller set of files than the plan names — you were handed the plan; it is the authority on scope, not your own estimate of what a minimal fix would touch. If you believe the plan names more files than the work needs, that is a finding about the PLAN: raise it as an ADVISORY note beginning 'SPEC:'. Live failure, 2026-08-14: a reviewer rejected a change for "modifying 6 files when the prescribed minimal fix requires only 2" against a plan that named FIVE — every one of which the implementer changed, and no others. Obeying the plan was the thing being rejected, so no attempt could ever pass, and the story burned its whole ladder.

Anything failing these is ADVISORY. Advisory findings are still valuable — they make the change smaller, clearer or safer — but they do not reject the work.

Judge the FIX ITSELF as a blocker freely: it does not address the prescribed root cause, it is materially larger than the PLAN OF RECORD — measured against the files and changes that plan names, never against a smaller fix you would have written instead, it removes a property the existing code guaranteed, it is unsafe, or it introduces a type error that breaks the build. For MOCK3-1 (fare boundary), a blocker must address the exact comparison operator in src/fares.ts and ensure test coverage spans the boundary age. For MOCK3-2 (schedule rendering), a blocker must address the loop bound in src/schedule.ts and ensure the final stop is included in the departure board output. Those are yours to enforce.
